messages.content: Can you retrieve the weather forecast for White Plains for next week with temperatures in Celsius?

function.name: requests_get
function.description: Sends a GET request to the specified URL to retrieve weather data from the Open-Meteo API. Note that the provided function is in Python 3 syntax.

url.description: URL of the Open-Meteo API endpoint.

headers.description: Headers to include in the request. Each key-value pair represents a header field and its value.

Content-Type.description: The MIME type of the body of the request (used with POST and PUT requests).

Accept.description: Media type(s) that is/are acceptable for the response.

timeout.description: Maximum time in seconds to wait for the server to send data before giving up. This is a float type value.

params.description: Query parameters for the GET request.

latitude.description: Latitude of the location, positive for N and negative for S. This is a float type value.

longitude.description: Longitude of the location, positive for E and negative for W. This is a float type value.

elevation.description: Elevation in meters above sea level for the location. The default value represents no elevation downscaling.

auth.description: Authentication tuple for HTTP authentication, in the format (username, password).

cert.description: Path to the SSL client certificate file (.pem). A null value means no client certificate is used.

cookies.description: Dictionary of cookies to send with the request. Each key represents a cookie name.

proxies.description: Dictionary mapping protocol names to the URL of the proxy. Each key-value pair represents a protocol and its proxy URL.

stream.description: If True, the response should be streamed; otherwise, it should be downloaded immediately.

verify.description: Whether to verify the server's TLS certificate.

message.reasoning:
We need to call the function requests_get with appropriate params. The user wants forecast for next week for White Plains. We need to find latitude and longitude for White Plains. White Plains is a city in New York, USA. Coordinates roughly 41.0535°N, 73.7629°W. So latitude=41.0535, longitude=-73.7629. They want temperatures in Celsius. The Open-Meteo API returns temperature in Celsius by default? I think yes. But we can specify "temperature_unit=celsius". Also we need to get forecast for next week. That means daily forecast for next 7 days. We can use "daily=temperature_2m_max,temperature_2m_min" maybe. Or "hourly=temperature_2m" but daily is simpler. We also need to set "forecast_days=7" or "start_date" and "end_date". Let's check typical usage: For daily forecast, you can specify "daily=temperature_2m_max,temperature_2m_min" and "timezone=America/New_York". And "start_date" and "end_date" can be omitted to get current day onward. But we want next week. We can set "start_date" to tomorrow's date. But we don't have date. We can just request daily forecast for next 7 days. The API will return daily data for next 7 days. So we can set "daily=temperature_2m_max,temperature_2m_min" and "forecast_days=7". The "forecast_days" param might not exist. Actually the API uses "forecast_days" as a query param. Yes, "forecast_days" is a parameter. So we can set "forecast_days=7". Also "timezone=America/New_York".

Thus the function call:

{
  url: "https://api.open-meteo.com/v1/forecast",
  headers: { "Content-Type": "application/json", "Accept": "application/json" },
  timeout: 10.0,
  params: {
    latitude: 41.0535,
    longitude: -73.7629,
    daily: "temperature_2m_max,temperature_2m_min",
    timezone: "America/New_York",
    forecast_days: 7
  }
}

But the function signature expects "params" to be an object with keys: latitude, longitude, elevation. It doesn't mention daily, timezone, forecast_days. But the description says "Query parameters for the GET request." It lists only latitude, longitude, elevation. But we can pass additional ones. The function signature may allow arbitrary keys. We'll pass them anyway.

Thus we call the function.
